title: Children’s Experiences of Neighborhood Food Environments, Eating Practices, and Subjective Well-Being: A Participatory Qualitative Study in Chile
content: Background/Objectives: Food environments shape children’s eating practices yet lived experiences remain insufficiently understood. This study explored how children and adolescents experience neighborhood food environments in relation to dimensions of subjective well-being in a context of social vulnerability in Chile. Methods: A quali-tative participatory study was conducted with 15 children and adolescents aged 12–15 years in La Legua and Carmen Mena, San Joaquín. Data were generated through Pho-tovoice, interviews, and emotional mapping. Photographs, maps, transcripts, and field notes were integrated and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis, complemented by spatial analysis of emotional maps. Results: Five themes were identified: proximity, mobility, and safety; availability, diversity, and food procurement; food as an affective, familial, and social experience; children’s agency; and tensions among practices, pref-erences, restrictions, and aspirations. Nearby food outlets facilitated access, whereas insecurity constrained mobility. Multiple points of sale did not necessarily translate into food diversity, with circuits centered on bread, beverages, snacks, sweets, and fast food. Food experiences included pleasure, care, recognition, togetherness, security, and relief, alongside concern and distress. Children selected, purchased, prepared, and evaluated food within family, economic, and territorial constraints. Conclusions: Neighborhood food environments were experienced as territorial, social, and affective spaces. Access depended not only on availability and proximity but also on safety, prices, mobility, family relationships, preferences, and situated agency. Participatory approaches can broaden nutrition research by revealing how children experience and negotiate food environments.
